projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Gilbert Lawrinson was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: I went in in November of '42, just before Thanksgiving Day -- around there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Drafted?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Oh, no. No. No draft. They were all volunteers and volunteers for the PTs, you know. Yeah. That's all we could say, all the guys were drafted -- no drafted hardly in the Navy. We thought it was more glamorous than we thought. We --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you train?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Great Lakes. Great Lakes, Illinois. Yeah. We had an old buddy of mine there, too and he was on -- it was Campbell. I don't know if he's still living or not. I tried to look him up when we went to St. Louis. He started on the U.S.S. Iowa, that big battleship, you know. Quite a bit of action on that ship. Yeah. He was telling me a story one time. He was up in what we call the crow's nest up high and all, a big ladder. And he seen the wake in the water. Found out it was a torpedo headed right for it. He gave -- signalled the bridge to turn, he said, or otherwise they would have got hit broadside. Yeah. Quite an experience, I tell you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were starting to tell me your job and when you went overseas.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job on the PT boat?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: I was rated -- well, I wasn't on the boats all the time. See, I was on base mostly, but -- well, that's another story, what happened. But, anyway, mostly base, but I made patrols with our squadron, see. And this particular night in action, where they had the man killed that was with the other squadron, with Squadron 21. I didn't know these guys, see, of course, then by name, of course. The guy who was killed was just killed more or less getting acquainted before that -- before we went in action, before that happened.

I noticed he was shot up pretty bad. It was this boy from Cincinnati, First Class Quarter Master. I looked back there, he was telling me about a time, the skipper, he was on some other ship or something before he got in our PTs, and the skipper let him dock one of the big boats or big ships. You know, dock, bringing it in, you know. It was quite a thing for him. Especially them big ships, they are pretty long, pretty big. Yeah. That was a real nice bunch of guys though. Well, we had 12 million when I was in that squadron. We had the Vandenboke (ph) brothers.

They both passed away now. One committed suicide several years ago, they tell me. And Ed Mahally (ph) and quite a few lieutenants. There was 12 million of us. And there was one fellow, he had stolen a fleet of boats in California, like the skip up -- boat I made patrols with in our squadron, and one flying five out. And John Wayne come on board one night. I got his autograph. Won't you know I lost -- showed it around and all and lost it somehow. Yeah. He was a big guy. I'll never forget it. I said, "Well, will you give me your autograph, John?" I ________ boy.

I tore it off. A big guy. And they were taking him off. They had some scouts -- some Australian scouts were taking him up, and they all found them a little sub machine gun, you know. Taking him off to let him off on an island at ___________ to put on a USO show. And they gave them coverage, you know, let them out, because you never know, thought they might get sniper attacks, you know. Had the guy in the turrets. Just getting ready. But that was quite an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you based over there?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Mostly New Guinea and the Shetland Islands. A little island about a mile and a half long was the last one I was based. I got sick there and had malaria. I got malaria. Got it bad. Went into my nervous system. I even got attacks after I come back home, I remember. But this little island, a mile and a half long, claim that __________ was the first white woman on the island. The natives used to bury their dead.

They had a little thatched roof over a grave, you know, and we'd build our tents around it. Yeah. It was something. Yeah. They brought Bob Hope over on one of our PTs in the squadron. In fact, the guy was telling me, and he later -- he got a degree from South Carolina, a big university in South Carolina. And we used to beat them at the time. And he got some engineering degree from there. So they brought him over on this boat, he was telling me. He said -- yeah, he said Bob Hope was telling us -- he quipped, you know, he was always joking. He says, "I had quite a ride over.

We only touched water twice." That was about right. We really took off or something, you know. Like I say, it wasn't about -- oh, I figure it was a mile and an eight to a knot, so we were going about -- at 47 knots, you figure about miles an hour, which is pretty fast. Of course this man was dying at the time. Yeah. That was quite an experience I tell you. You know, that's why I say them unusual stories seem to stick with you, you know. Life does go on, but that was a heck of an experience.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You want to go ahead and tell that story that's in that that you have written there?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Yeah. I have two stories.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tell both of them.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Tell one of them. Yeah. Well, you have them written down, but to tell it as it was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I have a copy.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Copies of them, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You want to read these or just tell them in your own words?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Well, maybe I could read them, because I might miss something that's there. What would you say about 300 words there. No. No. 200 words, maybe, something like that, huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: See, I was hoping I would get one out of PT. We have a PT magazine, a newsletter, like that they send out every few months or something, see. I got one lately. And I was going to contact the organization, tell them I would like to have them put in maybe the next issue, see. Maybe in February. Well, this is the one about "The Ride of My Life." It was in late January or early February 1944. I couldn't remember exact dates, you know, because I kept no diary. Every day seemed the same, you know, out there. I was stationed at the PT Boat Base at Dreger Harbor, New Guinea, near Finschhafen, if I'm saying that right.

And I was a Rear Man, Third Class on RON 12. One of the warrant officers asked if I would be willing to make a patrol with a boat from RON 21, a squadron which operated with RON 12, as they needed another man. I said I would go because it did not make any difference if I was on the boats or served on the base force, as we're all out there to put our lives on the line to save our great country. That's just the way I felt about it, you know. I was getting acquainted with a Quarter Master, First Class, named Harvey Donahue, who later died from his injuries. I was the 20-millimeter crew at the stern of the boat, and Harvey was assigned to fire the 30-millimeter up near the bow. You know, the bow of the boat. That was small enough now.

And Harvey was shot up pretty badly. And the skipper of our boat asked me to get some water for him. Because it was laying up there by the deck. We had a little life raft up near the deck. And I found later why he couldn't get up. So I had returned with the water. Because we were traveling at about 47 knots, I was supposed to crawl on my hands and knees to get back to him with the water. After that we raced to a base that had a doctor. He came aboard and cut Harvey's foot off above the ankle, then turned and handed the shoe to me with his foot still in it, and said, "Throw it over the side." I remember dropping it gently over the side, near the torpedo racks, on the starboard side, facing out to sea here. But then when I returned to the bow the doctor had just pronounced him dead.

Before returning to our base we had to secure his body to the small life raft near the bow of the boat, but I was slipping so bad in his pool of blood, so much that another crew member had to finish securing his leg with rope to the raft. Harvey and I were going to get together for a visit after the war, as he was from Cincinnati, Ohio and I was from Cleveland, but I never -- guess it was never meant to be. And I signed my name. Yeah. Yeah. Something like that I never forget. Guys, I showed a story to -- in our bowling place, you know. One guy just passed away. He had seen a lot of action in World War II. Got a battle star early. And he had been shot up -- his legs were shot up pretty bad, you know, and so he's sort of bowlegged, you know. And he told me about it.

He had seen a lot of action. And he read the stories. I says, I thought they was that unusual. A lot of guys die in action, but something like these were a little different, you know what I mean. Meeting your brother, that was something, too. That's this one about him now. "Reunion With My Oldest Brother." About March of 1944 -- I know this happened in action before he came out, because I know it was around, say, March, before my birthday, which I would have been 21 at that time. And this is before he came. I was telling him about it. So in 1944 a call came to our base in Dreger Harbor, New Guinea, that a duty officer asked if I had a brother I hadn't seen for awhile.

I told him that I had three brothers -- two brothers were in, of course, but the one brother that wasn't in he was a foreman at ___________ that I had not seen for almost a year. He handed me the phone and it was my oldest brother, Charles. I told him to come over to see our base -- our base, yeah. He was stationed at an Army base about two miles from Dreger Harbor. About two miles from our base. He did come out and was delighted to see each other. I asked an officer if he could stay for dinner and he said he could. We shared a quart bottle of Foster beer with our meal. That Foster beer from Australia, you know, every time I see it it reminds me of that story. As each man at our base was entitled to three quarts. It was cooled and we really enjoyed it. My brother Chuck loved beer, so it was the right time for him to visit.

A few days later I visited his Army base, but then we moved up the cost to Hollandia, New Guinea. About half way up the coast to another base and Chuck was moved to the Philippines. We didn't meet again until after the war was over. That was quite a story. Be over there about 10,000, 8,000 miles away and meet your brother only two miles away. You know, I bet the -- like I say, I can't think of anybody else have had that happen to, you know what I mean. He was so close and he came over to visit a few of our guys and some of us from the Chicago area and they had dinner. That was something. You could get a good meal. Tell this one cook and he'd feed them good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did your family back home say when they heard about that meeting?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Yeah. They couldn't believe it. Yeah. I remember -- I didn't tell them much about the story because, you know, I'm a truthful guy. I talk a lot so I'm -- you remember more of the good times than you do the bad times, any guy. I don't care what experience he's had. There's always a little time for -- even if he's been going bananas, you know, you think of some of the good things that happened. This was one of the good experiences. And of course every time we went to Australia, you know, it was wine, women and song. I told him, I says, "Didn't meet that new gal, did you?" I says, "No. How many did you have?" Yeah.

This old guy from Georgia, quite a guy. We had a lot of fun. He retired after the chief yeoman, which does the secretary work in there. In the Army they call them quarter master. So he's been around. Oh, this Admiral Holly (ph) died, one of the greatest naval officers of all time. I got a book there about him. He wrote three books. Been all over the world three times. Retired a rear admiral. Put 29 years in the Navy. He was one of Kennedy's campaign chairmen when he run for president. Of course the guys got good jobs in Washington, you know. Commander Buckley (ph), the man that passed away, was the guy that saved MacArthur's life, you know. That was the story of the war.

Remember they picked up MacArthur and they got him to -- probably, I don't know, quite a few miles anyway, three or 400 miles or more miles. Got him off there and then they picked him up and flew him to Australia, see. So the other part of that story, hell, the Sea Wolf comes by, so ___________ ___________ I'm about six feet. So he used to call him Johnny. Say, "Johnny, when you get in do me another favor." Says, "Pick up that person in the Philippines ___________. So this was about six months -- six weeks or so. So he did. He arranged to pick him up at the crack of dawn from___________. Got them now, see.

So after awhile we been there settled, the commander come down, to a big banquet. Well, we went down there and there was all beautiful and all, gold braids and all. He was going to take -- can't imagine at that time. And so he goes out there. Sit around the banquet table. He says, "Yeah. And thank you, Father, for Seawolf(ph) for saving my life. Here he was all in heaven and he didn't recognize him all cleared up. It was something. That's how they happened to invent the Seawolf(ph). He was a guy -- wide as a dog. Big bully guy. I seen him when he was eighty years old at Pittsburg. He died a few years ago, 84. But he was a big man and he had no blood and guts like Patton was, you know. Yeah.

It was quite a thing. This Bowling(ph) was the commander of all the PTs at that time. And used to call and say, hey, admiral -- well, he had a vice admiral, that's what Buckley(ph) retired from, and a little bit higher rank, but Holly(ph) here was rear admiral. Oh, same thing -- same rank. So you can manage the itenary and the pensions they must have had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you say what your specific job was? What was your job?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: His job or my --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your job.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: My job. Radar -- well radar man, third class, see. I was a seaman for a while, then they gave me the rate of radar man. I worked in the shop -- radar shop, and check out the units, you know, just like -- you know, you got just like your radar there -- your spare part where you got to put the other unit in there, see. And I made some patrols with a 195 boat. And I remember one time calling off the readings on the chart -- we were operating on a five-mile range. Got a five-mile, a 20-mile and 75. 75 was the farthest they figure they would be away from the base, right. And mostly five or 20.

And one time there was a big rock in the water, I say like from here to that side of where the driveway is out there. And I said, "Boy, that's getting pretty close." So he turned. We looked like our rudder was pretty close up to hit her there. That was something how clearly it could pick it up. Actually, I mean, radar was the front runner for television. That's how television -- you know, they seen what they could do with radar. Because now the big guns or big ships are radar controlled. You know, how they set the targets, you know, for the radar. And, of course, they are more sophisticated today now, but even then. So that was ___________ because they had a guy come out from ____________ corporation I think that made that radar up there in Massachusetts.

And he worked in the shop and he made -- he was in the picture called the Double Boats. He's mentioned in there, too. And I would have been on that boat, but the first man killed in our squadron. As a matter of fact, I might have next to him. I would been on that gun crew on a 40-millimeter. And he got killed. Bolt went right through him or something. And they tried to take him with the destroyer. And destroyers are pretty fast running ship, and they outrun them, see. So that was a bad thing. But what happened to me, it was a little while to ________ Island, where we went through maneuvers, off Panama.

There was a base about 16 miles off the coast of Panama. And on the weekends, you know, you go over in this little Spanish village over there. So I got a little too much tequila and I bring back some beer. That was a no-no. So they said, "Who brought the beer back." So I told them I did. Oh, they say, "Well, that's against the rules," you know. And he was reading the riot act to me. So he sent me to the old man, Admiral Holly(ph). Commander of the staff says, "You know, Lawrinson, that's the rules." So he did. He took me off the boats, which is probably what saved my life out there. So I was on base force after that, see.

But I say, what the heck. The base _______________ one time. We're all out there taking a chance, you know what I mean. Only them guys are more on the front line -- out on the boats are in the action. In fact, I would say they are closer a lot of times than the Army guys. You know, from here to the driveway away from you, you know, pretty close, out in the water, a moving target. So we got -- out of squadron there's only two squadron that got the presidential citation; Squadron 12 and 21. I'll show you the papers here. Got it right from the Secretary of the Navy. So it was quite an elite squadron.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was this issued?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: This was -- well, in '47. I got papers on it -- when they sent it to me right after the war I showed it to my wife -- my late wife.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any other particularly vivid memories of that time overseas?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Yeah. Overseas, sure. In Australia. That was nice. Met some nice people there. And I was there three different times, remember. One time, see, the seasons are just the opposite out here. When we're having spring here, like you need a jacket. You know, need a little old jacket -- you know, heavy shirt in the spring time. Their summer. Now we're going to come into winter, they are having summer. See the seasons -- it was 120 degrees the day we left there -- left Australia to come back here.

Imagine that. You see some of them guys on the Army ship crippled up, you know, and everything. They have malaria and combat fatigue, you know. So they check us out and see if we're that bad off. We weren't crazy enough, so we got released. Mustered out in Frisco, and met a buddy of mine. Of course, he passed away now. One of the best buddies. I knew his whole family for 60 years.

And he had an operation, a surgery on his knee. And they wouldn't put him on combat, see, so they put him on the sea coast artillery, more or less for protecting the Golden Gate, see. So we -- I remember we roomed together for a couple of days there he was operated. And he was showing me Chinatown and all of Frisco and rode the cable car.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about letters from home? Mail call.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Yeah. Letters from home, yeah. Yeah. Getting letters from home. I had a little card -- Christmas card that I sent them and I kept that as a souvenir. And it was -- they had a double dunker bunk -- when they got rid of -- I remember -- I say the old hammock day. Oh, anybody who had to sleep on a hammock, they are hard to get used to. They can give them back to the idiots. After they got through replacing then they put these double deck bunks on. They were a lot better. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you come back? When did you come home?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Well, that was in the spring of '45. Yeah. And the war was over a few months later, you know. Yeah. I think I was home whenever President Roosevelt died. Died about three days before my birthday. My birthday is April 15th. I got a one-day extension because that's income tax day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction around when you were home when Roosevelt died?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Yeah. Like all sad. He was a great leader. One of the greatest presidents we ever had. He was like the father of the country, you know. They had radio -- I mean they had radio fireside chats. They didn't have television then. They were just coming -- you know, seeing what they could do with radar and that was the front runner for television, see. Now it's really sophisticated.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you came back were you then out of the Navy or you were --

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: When I come out? Oh yeah. Discharged. We were discharged.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were discharged?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In spring of '45?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I come back. My brother -- I had two brothers that were still in yet. And they got -- a few months later, then they got out, too. One was in New Guinea and he went to the Philippines. And then my oldest brother was in Europe and he was lucky. He hurt his knee or something. Was going to go up in the Battle of the Bulge, and they kind of got jammed -- something in his knee, injured his knee, and they put him back, and he was in Eisenhower's headquarters, the secretary. Who knows, that probably could have saved his life. If he been on the Battle of the Bulge. That was a tough battle they tell me, I hear. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were back home when they dropped the atom bomb, then -- the first atom bomb, right?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: When was that, August? Yeah. I was home at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. What was the reaction back here to that?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Oh, that. Yeah. Well, they figured it was all happy because the whole idea, any serviceman knows is to save a lot of lives. If they had of went down there and tried and_________. They were dug in, you know, and big ships, you know, helped give them problems, but still to send troops in there, could have lost a lot more men, you know. So wanted to help finish the war off and save a lot of men's lives. That was a good thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after the Navy?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: No. Not too much. No. It took you awhile, you know, at first. You know, you start getting better food than over there. At times you had K rations. Yeah. Ate good at ________ over there at holiday time, you know. Got a good company steward tries to get us good chicken, cigars. It was good. They always got fed pretty good, but, I say, as time went on, on patrol ate K rations. You're hungry as a bear and fire up K rations one night.

Like I say, you know, it was no better off than some of the Army guys. It was pretty rough going and rugged duty. I'll grant you that. And the Navy Seal stuff -- we had a guy ______, our ________. And he served in the Navy Seals. We called them frogmen. That was a tough _______. Yeah. Yeah. He went through a lot. He said, "They walled have to hypnotize me to do that again."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did the frogmen ride with you on the PT boats?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Oh, no. No. They were separate -- are a separate outfit. Just like PTs are separate -- separate outfit. And then, of course, there's submariners, see. Submariners are something else. Guy can't stand it down below, usually strict discipline. We had a guy that served with them once and he talked back to an officer and they threw him out. Can't have that, you know, they are in real close quarters. Got to get along or get out, you know. And here he wasn't much reputation, either. You salute them -- say hello to all the officers, you know, salute them ______________.

And every once in a while -- very little regimentation, you see. And they knew the officers just like the enlisted men. Had some big guys there, yeah. Nicest fellow of all the squad -- the officers we had was Sy Taylor. He was a quarter master -- not a quarter -- a quarterback for Yale University. Had some big bony guys all right. And he was -- he was a lieutenant, come back from the morning, going for our briefing, you know. Go, "Good morning." Salute him and all. _______________ used to bullshit with the guys.

They would come back off patrols in the morning. Especially one of the guys in 196 -- some of them guys still come to reunion and see -- guys -- you know, them Vanderbilts(ph) -- Vanderbilt(ph) playboys, you know. In fact, he used to get letters from___________. Guy is reading the letter, his _______________. I remember that. But stuff like that. It was a great outfit, I tell you. Really nice guys. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other memories or stories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Yeah. Well, let's see. Of course, there was a special story -- especially to Australia that was nice. We took -- we went with the girls, asking want to go to see the bears -- what the hell is that bear? Koala bears. They lad a Koala bear park where they go. It was nice. It took a little -- they give us a bus trip there and ride around, the USOs took me a visit. It was nice. It was real good duty. Had street cars, call them ______ market. Like -- something like them cable cars.

They go along, and running boys, you know, they could walk off and jump off when they want. And I remember the conductor, he had a big pocketbook and he would check on your pass and all that. And, of course, we rode free, you know. Everybody was free. Of course, when I was in New York somebody always want to buy you a drink, you know. Panama was another place. That was a tough city, that Panama City.

We were supposed to be off the streets at 11:00 o'clock, and 10:30 in Balboa, see. Some of these guys they get mixed up -- get mixed up and they picked you up and detain you, you know. {Coughs} -- excuse me. That was a tough city. A red light district, you know. That's the Coconut Grove, whatever they call it. Had orders from home and for _____________________________________________. That was really something. Yeah. This one guy told me a story, he was with the city, in fact, or a ________ up there in Murray Hill (ph), telling about the time he was in Italy. It's par for the course in a lot of foreign countries, you know.

And the story he tells about the -- went into the town this one night -- some little town in Italy, and little kid comes along and says, "Hey, soldier." Says, "You want a drink?" He said, "I don't drink." Said, "I can get you a good bottle." He said, "No. No." "Hey, soldier, want cigarettes? I'll get you cigarettes." Said, "No. I don't smoke." Then said, "I'll get you a nice woman, beautiful woman." Says, "No." And the kid looked up and said, "Hey, soldier, what the fuck you come to town for?" That's all a sight. Out pimping for their sisters. You know the only reason ____________. A lot of them are like that. Well, you didn't see that much, tell you what my friend. But in Panama, a dime a dozen, all over the place, you know.

They don't realize, you know, it's -- I mean, the malls are, you know, way different now. I'll never forget that. What the hell you come to town for. Yeah. We -- it was a great experience, I tell you. I say we're lucky we come back and can tell about it. But I say it was great. People are nice. Australia was something. It was nice. So far away, but nice country. It really saved us in Australia, having them, you, know, for back -- because they had the -- Seventh Fleet had their headquarters in Brisbane, one of the cities about the middle of the coast, halfway between side any and Balboa, in there. And you're right at home there, you know, people treat us.

"Cherrio, Yank." It was great. Now there's a story -- I don't think -- he don't know, because I was with the original squadron, he wasn't, see. Some of these were replacements. I didn't know that for a few years. We had 27 guys that would show up at one of our reunions, or better. We got the attendance -- the most in attendance six years in a row. And that was quite a thing.

I couldn't figure out why. Now I see more of these guys came in later in the squad. They weren't original. See, I was one of the originals. And I says, you know, we had one Indian boy and one black guy. He didn't know that. Say, "You know that?" Yeah. I said, "I didn't know it." When he got back the black guy was from -- guy named Lay, he was from Detroit. And, see, in them days, he was just a mess cook, an orderly like today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: You know, they didn't have no rank, see. But now that's all changed. But the Indian boy --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many PT boats were in a squadron?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: About 12 in our squadron. About 12.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And there were, you say --

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: 45 squadrons.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- 45 squadrons?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Between the Atlantic and the Pacific, yeah. That's quite a lot. 16,000 men between then and officers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How big was the crew on a PT boat?

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: Most of them had about 12, 15. Surprised they got that many on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Gilbert Lawrinson
sp.p: And they were just on a boat.
[END OF TAPE; CONCLUSION OF INTERVIEW]
